name: Hai//om-Akhoe
world_status: statement found in an open source
sweep_summary: Hai//om-Akhoe (haio1238) is not in the catalog. The sweep's single title-keyword hit, Schmidt 1986 'Tales and beliefs about eyes-on-his-feet', is a comparative Khoisan folklore paper (Buske, QKF 4) - a spurious hit, irrelevant to word stress, not retrieved. Beyond it, the material already on file from the earlier audit pass was re-read: Rapold & Widlok 2008 (SAH 20, open MPI PuRe postprint) describes Haiǁom/ǂĀkhoe word prosody as lexical tone on bimoraic stems and says nothing about stress; Hoymann 2010 and Widlok 2008 are likewise silent.com returned 403, and sahumanities.org PDFs require subscription, so the one likely locus of an explicit stress statement - Widlok's Haiǁom sketch (phonology pp.56-58) in Vossen (ed.) 2013 The Khoesan Languages (Google Books id QvpwwRLYai0C, partial preview) - could not be opened; it is the high-priority acquisition, with Heikkinen's unpublished ǂAkhoen sketch second. Wikipedia's Khoekhoe page carries an unreferenced 'first syllable receives the most stress' line for Standard Khoekhoe, which is a different variety and not a citable source. No first-hand word-stress statement for Haiǁom was read. Receipts appended to (new xml).

earlier_scan.source_named: Doke, Clement M. 1925 grammar sketch (Glottolog MED for haio1238); Haiǁom is Khoekhoe-lectal — no stress description reachable online

new_statements.quote: [p.137] This section investigates the basic tonology of three Northern Khoekhoe varieties and compares them with Central ('Standard') Khoekhoe ... Based on new data on these little known peripheral varieties, we attempt to show similarities as well as differences across the Khoekhoe cluster in the specific linguistic domain of word prosodic systems. [p.141] ... the following discussion is limited to nouns, but verbs behave in exactly the same way tonally. [p.148] ... we need four tonal levels for Tsumeb Damara, even if only the six main patterns ('the big Six') are taken into consideration. Exactly the same level realisations are found in the ǂĀkhoe and Hai‖om for the patterns A, B, E and F, although they are not illustrated here for lack of space.

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: File checked: (30 pp., MPI PuRe open postprint) and. All three quoted fragments are present verbatim at the stated locators: p.137 (pdf p.5; txt l.211-216) 'This section investigates the basic tonology of three Northern Khoekhoe varieties and compares them with Central ('Standard') Khoekhoe... in the specific linguistic domain of word prosodic systems'; p.141 (txt l.366-367) 'the following discussion is limited to nouns, but verbs behave in exactly the same way tonally'; p.148 (pdf p.16; txt l.520-526) 'we need four tonal levels for Tsumeb Damara, even if only the six main patterns ('the big Six') are taken into consideration. Exactly the same level realisations are found in the ǂĀk…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Haiǁom / ǂĀkhoe word prosody is described purely as lexical tone: each bimoraic stem carries a two-tone citation melody (six major patterns cognate with Central Khoekhoe), realised with four distinctive tone levels, and a derived sandhi melody in non-initial position of the tonological phrase. The source makes no statement about word stress or accent; no stress placement rule is given anywhere in the accessible literature.
new_statements.exceptions: Minor/exceptional tone melodies exist beyond the six major patterns (not a stress matter). In ǂĀkhoe the noun citation form carries the oblique marker -a and the declarative particle ge takes its tone from the preceding stem by spreading.
new_statements.domain_note: Lexical/word-level tone on bimoraic stems; citation melody (phrase-initial, isolation, '__ ge' frame) vs sandhi melody (non-initial in tonological phrase). Data: two Outjo Haiǁom speakers with Etosha roots; ǀGomais (Mangetti West) ǂĀkhoe speakers; whistled and spoken elicitation.
new_statements.identity_note: Rapold & Widlok 2008 describe two lects that Glottolog merges under haio1238 'Hai//om-Akhoe': Outjo Haiǁom (two speakers with Etosha-pan roots) and ǀGomais (Mangetti West) ǂĀkhoe, plus Tsumeb (Ghaub) Damara, which is a Khoekhoe (nama1264-side) transitional dialect, not Haiǁom. Two bibliographic traps for this key: (a) Doke 1925 'Chû: Bushmen of north-west Kalahari' (the earlier scan's named source, Glottolog MED) is a computerized Glottolog assignment and does not describe Khoekhoe Haiǁom; (b) Werner 1906's 'Heikum' at the Omuramba Omatako spoke a Ju/!Xun lect by his own wordlist and statement, not Khoekhoe Haiǁom.

new_statements.quote: Following the authors listed, and as described in detail by Haacke (1999a), each Khoekhoe stem of most lexical categories has two main tone patterns, whose distribution is mainly conditioned by the position of a word in a tonological phrase. [...] As in many other Khoisan languages, the canonical CV shape of lexical stems is bimoraic and has the shape C1V(C2)V, where in the case of Khoekhoe C2 = /p, r, m, n/. This means that, depending on the analysis, most lexical stems bear two tones or a contour tone.
new_statements.citation: Rapold, Christian J. & Thomas Widlok (2008). Dimensions of variability in Northern Khoekhoe language and culture. Southern African Humanities 20: 133-161.
new_statements.locator: pp.140-141 (tone section, Table 1 'Major citation form melodies in bimoraic stems'); levels p.148; Haiǁom-specific melodies pp.155-157
new_statements.reading: This is a TONE statement, not a stress statement: Haiǁom/ǂĀkhoe word prosody is described as lexical tone on bimoraic stems (six major citation melodies analysed as sequences of level tones over four contrastive levels, with citation vs sandhi alternation by phrase position). The article, the only first-hand phonological description of Haiǁom readable in this sweep, is silent on stress or accent placement; no first-hand word-stress statement for Haiǁom was found anywhere reachable. Best guess for coding: tone language, stress undescribed (the unreferenced Wikipedia 'first syllable' claim is for Standard Khoekhoe and is not a source).

sources.locator: section 'TONE', p.137 (opening) and p.148 (tone levels); also p.141
sources.note: Section 'TONE' (pp.137-157) treats the word-prosodic systems of ǀGomais ǂĀkhoe, Outjo Haiǁom and Tsumeb Damara as lexical tone: bimoraic C1V(C2)V stems carry two-tone citation melodies (six major patterns A-F), with four distinctive tone levels in ǂĀkhoe/Haiǁom (p.148); citation vs sandhi melody conditioned by position in the tonological phrase; verbs behave like nouns tonally. No mention of stress or accent anywhere.
